{{ill|calligrapher|WD=Q3303330}}; {{ill|philosopher|WD=Q4964182}}|father={{ill|Mitsuno Momoe|WD=Q118750033}}|notable_works={{ill|An Essay on the Protection of the Nation|WD=Q11450104}}; {{ill|The Regulations for the Students of the Mountain School|WD=Q134271462}}|religion={{ill|Tendai|WD=Q855964}}|native_name=最澄|resting_place={{ill|Enryaku-ji|WD=Q917195}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q449943]] Wikidata name: Saichō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:00, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|8/9th-century Japanese Buddhist monk; founder of the Tendai sect}} {{Over-quotation|date=July 2024}} {{Infobox religious biography |name = Saichō (最澄) |image= 最澄像 一乗寺蔵 平安時代.jpg |caption = Painting of Saichō |birth_date = September 15, 767 |birth_place = |death_date = June 26, 822 (age 54) | religion = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] |school = [[:en:Tendai|Tendai]] |title = Founder of [[:en:Tendai|Tendai Buddhism]] |teacher = Gyōhyō (行表) |successor = Gishin (義真) }} {{nihongo|'''Saichō'''|最澄||September 15, 767 – June 26, 822}} was a [[:en:Japanese people|Japanese]] [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monk]] credited with founding the [[:en:Tendai|Tendai]] school of Buddhism based on the Chinese [[:en:Tiantai|Tiantai]] school he was exposed to during his trip to [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] beginning in 804. He founded the temple and headquarters of Tendai at [[Enryaku-ji]] on [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] near [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He is also said to have been the first to bring [[:en:History of tea in Japan|tea]] to Japan. After his death, he was awarded the posthumous title of '''Dengyō Daishi''' (伝教大師). == Life == === Early life === Saichō was born in the year 767 in the city of Ōmi, in present [[:en:Shiga Prefecture|Shiga Prefecture]], with the given name of Hirono.{{cite web|title=Tendai Homepage: Dengyo Daishi's Life and Teachings|url=http://www.tendai.or.jp/english/index.php|access-date=10 December 2012}} According to family tradition, Saichō's ancestors were descendants of [[:en:Emperor of China|emperors]] of [[Han dynasty#Eastern Han|Eastern Han China]]; however, no positive evidence exists for this claim. The region where Saichō was born did have a large Chinese immigrant population, so Saichō likely did have Chinese ancestry.{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho: The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=17–37}} During Saichō's time, the Buddhist temples in Japan were officially organized into a national network known as the [[:en:Provincial temple|Provincial temple]] system, and at the age of 13, Saichō became a disciple of one Gyōhyō (722–797, 行表).{{cite book|editor1-last=Buswell|editor1-first=Robert Jr|editor2-last=Lopez|editor2-first=Donald S. Jr.|editor1-link=Robert Buswell Jr.|editor2-link=Donald S. Lopez, Jr.|title=Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism|page=737|date=2013|publisher=Princeton University Press|location=Princeton, NJ|isbn=9780691157863}}{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Gyohyo|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=955}} He took tonsure as a novice monk at the age of 14 and was given the ordination name "Saichō". Gyōhyō in turn was a disciple of [[:en:Dao-xuan|Dao-xuan]] (702–760, 道璿, Dōsen in Japanese), a prominent monk from China{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Tao-Hsien|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=2215|access-date=10 December 2012}} of the Tiantai school who had brought the [[:en:East Mountain Teaching|East Mountain Teaching]] of [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]], [[:en:Huayan|Huayan]] teachings and the [[:en:Bodhisattva Precepts|Bodhisattva Precepts]] of the [[:en:Brahmajala Sutra (Mahayana)|''Brahmajala Sutra'']] to Japan in 736 and served as the "precept master" for ordination prior to the arrival of [[:en:Jianzhen|Jianzhen]]. By the age of 20, he undertook the full [[:en:Prātimokṣa|monastic precepts]] at the [[Tōdai-ji]], thus becoming a fully ordained monk in the official temple system. A few months later he abruptly retreated to [[:en:Mount Hiei|Mount Hiei]] for an intensive study and practice of Buddhism, though the exact reason for his departure remains unknown. Shortly after his retreat, he composed his {{nihongo|''Ganmon''|願文||"Saichō's Prayer"}} which included his personal vows to: # So long as I have not attained the stage where my six faculties are pure, I will not venture out into the world. # So long as I have not realized the absolute, I will not acquire any special skills or arts [e.g. medicine, divination, calligraphy, etc.]. # So long as I have not kept all the precepts purely, I will not participate in any lay donor's Buddhist meetings. # So long as I have not attained wisdom (lit. ''hannya'' 般若), I will not participate in worldly affairs unless it be to benefit others. # May any merit from my practice in the past, present and future be given not to me, but to all sentient beings so that they may attain supreme enlightenment. In time, Saichō attracted other monks both on Mount Hiei, and from the Buddhist community in [[:en:Nara (city)|Nara]], and a monastic community developed on Mount Hiei, which eventually became [[Enryaku-ji]]. Saichō was said to have carved an image of the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaiṣajyaguru]] and enshrined it. Additionally, he lit a lamp of oil before the Buddha and prayed that the lamp would never be extinguished. This lamp is now known as the {{nihongo|''Fumetsu no Hōtō''|不滅の法灯||"Inextinguishable Dharma Lamp"}} and has remained lit for 1200 years. The capital of Japan was moved from Nara to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] in 784, and then to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] in 795. Because Mount Hiei was coincidentally located to the northeast of Kyoto, a direction considered dangerous according to [[:en:Feng shui|Chinese geomancy]], Saichō's presence on the mountain was thought to protect the new capital and brought him to the attention of the court. Saichō and his community on Mount Hiei also started to correspond and exchange ceremonies with the established communities in Nara, in addition to the monks at the Court, further enhancing his prestige. One of Saichō's earliest supporters in the Court was Wake no Hiroyo, who invited Saichō to give lectures at Takaosan-ji along with fourteen other eminent monks. Saichō was not the first to be invited, indicating that he was still relatively unknown in the Court, but rising in prominence. === Trip to China === [[File:Culto do chá p25.png|thumb|Saichō is known for having introduced tea to Japan]] The success of the Takaosanji lectures, plus Saichō's association with Wake no Hiroyo soon caught the attention of [[Emperor Kanmu]] who consulted with Saichō about propagating his Buddhist teachings further, and to help bridge the traditional rivalry between the [[:en:East Asian Yogācāra|East Asian Yogācāra]] and [[:en:East Asian Mādhyamaka|East Asian Mādhyamaka]] schools. The emperor granted a petition by Saichō to journey to China to further study Tiantai doctrine in China and bring back more texts.{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho : The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=38–64}} Saichō was expected to only remain in China for a short time however. Saichō could read Chinese but was unable to speak it at all, thus he was allowed to bring a trusted disciple along named {{nihongo|Gishin|義眞}}, who apparently could speak Chinese. Gishin would later become one of the head monks of the Tendai order after Saichō. Saichō was part of the four-ship [[:en:Japanese missions to Imperial China|diplomatic mission to Tang China]] in 803. The ships were forced to turn back due to heavy winds, where they spent some time at [[:en:Dazaifu, Fukuoka|Dazaifu, Fukuoka]]. During this time, Saichō likely met another passenger, [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]], a fellow Buddhist monk who was sent to China on a similar mission though he was expected to stay much longer. When the ships set sail again, two sank during a heavy storm, but Saichō's ship arrived at the port of [[:en:Ningbo|Ningbo]], then known as Mingzhou ({{zh|c=明州| p=Míngzhōu}}), in northern [[:en:Zhejiang|Zhejiang]] in 804. Shortly after arrival, permission was granted for Saichō and his party to travel to [[:en:Tiantai Mountain|Tiantai Mountain]] and he was introduced to the seventh Patriarch of [[:en:Tiantai|Tiantai]], Daosui ({{zh|c=道邃|p=Dàosuì}}), who became his primary teacher during his time in China. Daosui was instrumental in teaching Saichō about Tiantai methods of meditation, monastic discipline and orthodox teachings. Saichō remained under this instruction for approximately 135 days. Saichō spent the next several months copying various Buddhist works with the intention of bringing them back to Japan with him. While some works existed in Japan already, Saichō felt that they suffered from copyist errors or other defects, and so he made fresh copies. Once the task was completed, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo, but the ship was harbored in [[:en:Fuzhou|Fuzhou]] at the time, and would not return for six weeks. During this time, Saichō went to Yuezhou (越州, modern-day [[:en:Shaoxing|Shaoxing]]) and sought out texts and information on [[:en:Vajrayana|Vajrayana]] (Esoteric) Buddhism. The Tiantai school originally only utilized "mixed" ({{nihongo|''zōmitsu''|雑密||}}) ceremonial practices, but over time esoteric Buddhism took on a greater role. By the time Saichō had arrived in China, a number of Tiantai Buddhist centers provided esoteric training, and both Saichō and Gishin received initiation at a temple in [[:en:Yue Prefecture (Zhejiang)|Yue Prefecture]]. However, it's unclear what transmission or transmissions(s) they received. Some evidence suggests that Saichō did not receive the dual ({{nihongo|''ryōbu''|兩部||}} transmissions of the [[:en:Diamond Realm|Diamond Realm]] and the [[:en:Womb Realm|Womb Realm]]. Instead, it is thought he may have only received the Diamond Realm transmission, but the evidence is not conclusive one way or the other. Finally, on the tenth day of the fifth month of 805, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo and after compiling further bibliographies, boarded the ship back for Japan and arrived in [[:en:Tsushima, Nagasaki|Tsushima]] on the fifth day of the sixth month. Although Saichō had only stayed in China for a total of eight months, his return was eagerly awaited by the court in Kyoto. === Founding of Tendai === On his return from China, Saichō worked hard to win recognition from the court and "in the first month of 806, Saichō's Tendai Lotus school (''Tendai-hokke-shū'' 天台法華宗) won official recognition when the court of the ailing emperor Kanmu issued another edict, this one permitting two annual ordinands (''nenbundosha'') for Saichō's new school on Mount Hiei. This edict states that, following Saichō's request, the ordinands would be divided between two curricula: the ''shanagō'' course, centering on the study of the Mahavairocana Sūtra (this was the Mikkyō curriculum, shana being the abbreviation for Birushana, the Japanese transliteration of Vairocana), and the shikangō course, based on the study of the ''Mo-ho chih-kuan'', the seminal work of the T'ien-t'ai patriarch Chih-i 智顗 (538–597) (this was the Tendai curriculum, ''shikan'' being the Japanese reading of Chih-i's central practice of ''chih-kuan'' [cessation and contemplation]) (''Kenkairon engi'', DZ 1, pp. 294–296). Thus from its very inception the Tendai Lotus school was equally based on Mikkyō and T'ien-t'ai. It was as a subdivision of Saichō's new school that Mikkyō first received the official acknowledgment of the imperial court and became a proper subject of study in Japanese Buddhism. {{quote|[I]n 813 Saichō composed the ''Ehyō tendaishū'' (DZ 1, pp. 343–366), which argues that the principal Buddhist masters of China and Korea all relied on T'ien-t'ai doctrine in composing their own works. By identifying numerous references to and quotes from T'ien-t'ai treatises in the works of [[:en:Jizang|Chi-tsang]] 吉蔵 of the [[:en:East Asian Mādhyamaka|San-lun]] 三論 school, Chih-chou of the [[:en:East Asian Yogācāra|Fa-hsiang]] 法相 school, Fa-tsang of the [[:en:Huayan|Huayen]] 華嚴 school, I-hsing of [[:en:Mikkyō|Mikkyō]], and other prominent teachers, Saichō asserted that T'ien-t'ai formed the foundation for all major Buddhist schools in East Asia.Abe Ryūichi: Saichō and Kūkai: A conflict of interpretations. Japanese Journal of Religious Studies Vol: 22/1–2, pp. 103–137, 1995. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090219104325/http://www.nanzan-u.ac.jp/SHUBUNKEN/publications/jjrs/pdf/438.pdf PDF]}} Before Saichō, all monastic ordinations took place at [[Tōdai-ji]] temple under the ancient [[:en:Vinaya|Vinaya]] code, but Saichō intended to found his school as a strictly [[:en:Mahayana|Mahayana]] institution and ordain monks using the Bodhisattva Precepts only. Despite intense opposition from the traditional Buddhist schools in [[:en:Nara (city)|Nara]], his request was granted by [[:en:Emperor Saga|Emperor Saga]] in 822, several days after his death. This was the fruit of years of effort and a formal debate. === Decline and Death === By 822, Saichō petitioned the court to allow the monks at Mount Hiei to ordain under the Bodhisattva Precepts rather than the traditional ordination system of the ''[[:en:Prātimokṣa|Prātimokṣa]]'', arguing that his community would be a purely [[:en:Mahayana|Mahayana]], not [[:en:Hinayana|Hinayana]] one.{{cite book | last = Abe | first = Ryuichi | title = The Weaving of Mantra: Kukai and the Construction of Esoteric Buddhist Discourse | publisher = Columbia University Press | year = 1999 | isbn = 0-231-11286-6 | pages=40–44, 50–52}} This was met with strong protest by the Buddhist establishment who supported the ''kokubunji'' system, and lodged a protest. Saichō composed the {{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論||"A Clarification of the Precepts"}}, which stressed the significance of the Bodhisattva Precepts,{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Saicho|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=319|access-date=10 December 2012}} but his request was still rejected until 7 days after his death at the age of 56. == Relationship with Kūkai == Saichō traveled to China along with a number of other young monks, one of whom was named [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]]. Saichō befriended him during his trip to [[:en:China|China]] who traveled with him going and coming. This turned out to be pivotal to the future development of Buddhism. {{quote|During the last month of his stay on Chinese soil, while awaiting the arrival of his ship at the port city of Ming-chou, Saichō traveled to Yüeh-chou to collect additional Buddhist texts. At Lung-hsing ssu 龍興寺 Saichō chanced to meet the priest Shun-hsiao"}}, and likewise returned with esoteric ([[:en:Vajrayana|tantric]]) Buddhist texts. Saichō was entranced with the new material and wanted to learn more. On the trip back he found that Kukai had studied these teachings in depth and had an entire library of [[:en:Vajrayana|Vajrayana]] materials. This friendship would influence the future of Tendai. {{quote|Saichō 最澄 and Kūkai 空海 are renowned as the founders, respectively, of the Japanese Tendai and Shingon schools, both of which grew into influential institutions of continuing importance even today. The two figures cooperated, moreover, in an effort to transplant the seed of esoteric Buddhism (mikkyō) to the cultural soil of Japan. Saichō, for example, prepared the way for Kūkai—still largely unrecognized after his return from T'ang China—to perform the Mikkyō initiation ritual of [[:en:Abhisheka|''abhiṣeka'']] (''kanjō'' 灌頂) for the high priests of the Nara Buddhist establishment and the dignitaries of the imperial" [[:en:Heian-kyō|Heian court]].}} It was Saichō who performed the ''abhiṣeka'', or initiatory ritual, for the court. {{quote|Saichō also endorsed the court's bequest to Kūkai of the mountain temple of [[:en:Jingo-ji|Takaosan-ji]] northwest of Kyoto as the first center for Kūkai's [[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon Buddhism]]. Kūkai, in turn, responded to Saichō's wish to incorporate Mikkyō into the eclectic system of Tendai by training Saichō and his disciples in the esoteric Buddhist rituals and by lending Saichō various Mikkyō texts that he had brought with him from China."}} == The identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings == {{JapaneseBuddhism}} Thus esoteric Buddhism became an important aspect of the Tendai school, which was primarily focused on the [[:en:en:Lotus Sutra|en:Lotus Sutra]]. However, unlike the [[:en:Shingon Buddhism|Shingon]] school (which saw esoteric practice as superior to the Lotus Sutra), Saichō held to the "identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings" (''enmitsu itchi'' 円密一致) which means there is a unity and agreement among the teachings of the Lotus Sutra and Esoteric Buddhism."Ōkubo Ryōshun 大久保良峻. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/4331 “The Identity between the Purport of the Perfect and Esoteric Teachings.”] ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 41/1 (2014): 83–102. Saichō, in a letter to Kukai, wrote:Ryuichi Abe. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/2562 ''Saichō and Kūkai: A Conflict of Interpretations Ryuichi Abe.''] Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 1995 22/1-2
But the [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]] school (''shanashu'' 遮那宗) and Tendai interfuse with one another. They also share the same commentary.... There should be no such thing as preferring one to the other. The Lotus and the [[:en:Golden Light Sutra|Golden Light]] are those texts to which the previous emperor [[[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]]] devoted himself, and there exists no difference between the One Unifying Vehicle [of Tendai] and Shingon.
Paul Groner states, {{quote|Chinese T'ien-t'ai had been a syncretistic tradition, particularly at the T'ien-t'ai Yu-ch'uan monastery. Chinese monks had been interested in Ch'an and Esoteric Buddhism as well as in the Ssu-fen la and Fan wang precepts. Saichō inherited this tradition, but developed certain aspects of it in innovative ways. For example, Saichō considered Esoteric Buddhism to be essentially the same as Tendai (enmitsu itchi) and thus awarded Esoteric Buddhism a more central place in the Tendai tradition than it had been given by most Chinese monks. Like Kūkai, Saichō emphasized the importance of striving for enlightenment as an immediate goal to be attained in this existence (''sokushin-jōbutsu'').Groner, Paul (1989). "The Lotus Sutra and Saicho's Interpretation of the Realization of Buddhahood with This Very Body". In Tanabe, George J.; Tanabe, Willa Jane (ed.). The Lotus Sutra in Japanese Culture. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. {{ISBN|0-8248-1198-4}}. pp. 61–62}} Tendai and Esoteric practices, he felt, provided a direct path (''jikidō'') to enlightenment, whereas the teachings of the Nara schools required aeons to bring the practitioner to enlightenment.{{cite news | last = Groner | first = Paul | title = Short History of Dengyo Daishi | url = http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060503031218/http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-date = 2006-05-03}} However, {{quote|During the years that Saichō studied Esoteric Buddhism (from 805–815), more than half of the Tendai yearly ordinands left Mount Hiei. Many of them defected to the [[:en:East Asian Yogācāra|Hosso school]]; others departed in order to study Esoteric Buddhism with Kūkai or to support their ailing mothers. It became clear that if Tendai were to survive, Saichō would have to retain many more of his students on Mount Hiei.}} Moreover, Saichō began to realize that his own idea of "enmitsu itchi" was not exactly shared by the esoteric Shingon school, and especially its founder Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi). Ryuichi Abe writes, {{quote|[W]hat makes the relationship between Saichō and Kūkai decisive in Japanese Buddhist history is not so much their cooperation as the manner in which it came to an end. Their alliance began to deteriorate when Saichō, after receiving abhiseka from Kūkai, hurried back to Mount Hiei, where the work of laying the foundation of the new Tendai school awaited him. Saichō continued to study and copy Mikkyō texts borrowed from Kūkai, but despite Kūkai's repeated requests he did not return to Takaosan-ji to resume his studies. Their rapport finally terminated when Kūkai harshly condemned Saichō's approach to Mikkyō as a transgression of the esoteric precept of samaya [the promise to keep the oral/esoteric teachings private], and Saichō retorted by denouncing Kūkai's manner of instruction}} {{quote|Thus it was Mikkyō that brought Saichō and Kūkai together; it was also Mikkyō that drove them apart. The break between Saichō and Kūkai left a long-lasting legacy in the Tendai and Shingon schools, whose complex relationship, constantly oscillating between affiliation and rivalry, shaped the contours of Buddhist history in the Heian period.}} {{quote|During the last five or six years of his life, Saicho strove to secure the place of Tendai within Japanese Buddhism, and in the process composed almost all of his major works.}} {{quote|In 816, Saichō added a new introduction to the work. This introduction chides Sanron, Hossō, and Kegon—the leading schools of Nara Buddhism—for ignoring the influence of T'ien-t'ai on the works of their Chinese patriarchs, but its criticism of Shingon stands out: "The esoteric Shingon Buddhist, the newcomer, went so far as to deny the validity of transmission through writing (hitsuju Ù4)" (DZ 3, p. 344). In this comment Saichō denounced Kūkai and Shingon for their approach to Buddhism and religious study."}} Saichō's late life criticisms were ignored by his own leading disciples, and the Tendai would continue to teach Mikkyō and [[Buddhist meditation#Tiantai .C5.9Bamatha-vipa.C5.9Byan.C4.81|Shikangō]] (''śamatha-vipaśyanā''). Saichō's public condemnation of Kūkai would later form the seeds for some of the criticisms leveled by [[:en:Nichiren|Nichiren]] (1222–1282), the founder of [[:en:Nichiren Buddhism|Nichiren Buddhism]], who would cite that work in his own debates in the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]].Gosho | http://www.sgilibrary.org/view.php?page=565{{better source needed|date=July 2024}} Saichō was also an author. He wrote a number of texts, the main ones include: *{{nihongo|''Shōgon Jikkyō''|照権実鏡|}} (817) *{{nihongo|''Sange Gakushō Shiki''|山家学生式|}} (818–819) *{{nihongo|''Shugo Kokkai Shō''|守護国界章|}} (818) *{{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論|}} (820) ==See also== *[[:en:Tendai|Tendai]] *[[:en:Annen (monk)|Annen (monk)]] *[[:en:Ennin|Ennin]] == References == {{Reflist}} ==Further reading== * Pruden, Leo; Rhodes, Robert; trans. (1994). ''The Essentials of the Eight Traditions and The Candle of the Latter Dharma'', Berkeley, CA: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research. {{ISBN|0-9625618-7-8}} ==External links== *[https://web.archive.org/web/20130808031328/https://sites.google.com/site/dharmadepository/writings/saichos-reforms Saichō's Monastic Reforms] {{Japanese Buddhist Pantheon}} {{Buddhism topics}} [[en:Saichō]] [[az:Sayço]] [[cs:Saičó]] [[de:Saichō]] [[es:Saichō]] [[et:Saichō]] [[eu:Saichō]] [[fa:سایچو]] [[fr:Saichō]] [[id:Saichō]] [[it:Saichō]] [[ja:最澄]] [[ko:사이초]] [[nl:Saicho]] [[no:Saichō]] [[pl:Saichō]] [[pt:Saicho]] [[ro:Saichō]] [[ru:Сайтё]] [[sh:Saichō]] [[sl:Saičo]] [[sr:Саићо]] [[sv:Saichō]] [[tr:Saichō]] [[uk:Сайтьо]] [[vi:Tối Trừng]] [[zh:最澄]] {{wikidata link|Q449943}} [[Category:767 births]] [[Category:822 deaths]] [[Category:9th-century Japanese calligraphers]] [[Category:Founders of Buddhist sects]] [[Category:Japanese ambassadors to the Tang dynasty]] [[Category:Japanese Buddhist clergy]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:Tendai]] [[Category:Tendai Buddhist monks]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed parentheses]]

{{ill|calligrapher|WD=Q3303330}}; {{ill|philosopher|WD=Q4964182}}|father={{ill|Mitsuno Momoe|WD=Q118750033}}|notable_works={{ill|An Essay on the Protection of the Nation|WD=Q11450104}}; {{ill|The Regulations for the Students of the Mountain School|WD=Q134271462}}|religion={{ill|Tendai|WD=Q855964}}|native_name=最澄|resting_place={{ill|Enryaku-ji|WD=Q917195}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q449943]] Wikidata name: Saichō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:00, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|8/9th-century Japanese Buddhist monk; founder of the Tendai sect}} {{Over-quotation|date=July 2024}} {{Infobox religious biography |name = Saichō (最澄) |image= 最澄像 一乗寺蔵 平安時代.jpg |caption = Painting of Saichō |birth_date = September 15, 767 |birth_place = |death_date = June 26, 822 (age 54) | religion = {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} |school = {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} |title = Founder of {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai Buddhism}} |teacher = Gyōhyō (行表) |successor = Gishin (義真) }} {{nihongo|'''Saichō'''|最澄||September 15, 767 – June 26, 822}} was a {{ill|Japanese people|en|Japanese people|WD=Q161652|lt=Japanese}} {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=Buddhist monk}} credited with founding the {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} school of Buddhism based on the Chinese {{ill|Tiantai|en|Tiantai|WD=Q668188|lt=Tiantai}} school he was exposed to during his trip to {{ill|Tang dynasty|en|Tang dynasty|WD=Q9683|lt=Tang China}} beginning in 804. He founded the temple and headquarters of Tendai at [[Enryaku-ji]] on {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}} near {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. He is also said to have been the first to bring {{ill|History of tea in Japan|en|History of tea in Japan|WD=Q6579892|lt=tea}} to Japan. After his death, he was awarded the posthumous title of '''Dengyō Daishi''' (伝教大師).
== Life ==
=== Early life ===
Saichō was born in the year 767 in the city of Ōmi, in present {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}, with the given name of Hirono.<ref name="tendaishu">{{cite web|title=Tendai Homepage: Dengyo Daishi's Life and Teachings|url=http://www.tendai.or.jp/english/index.php|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> According to family tradition, Saichō's ancestors were descendants of {{ill|Emperor of China|en|Emperor of China|WD=Q268218|lt=emperors}} of [[Han dynasty#Eastern Han|Eastern Han China]];<ref name="tendaishu" /> however, no positive evidence exists for this claim. The region where Saichō was born did have a large Chinese immigrant population, so Saichō likely did have Chinese ancestry.<ref name="groner-book">{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho: The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=17–37}}</ref>
During Saichō's time, the Buddhist temples in Japan were officially organized into a national network known as the {{ill|Provincial temple|en|Provincial temple|WD=Q1207757|lt=Provincial temple}} system, and at the age of 13, Saichō became a disciple of one Gyōhyō (722–797, 行表).<ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Buswell|editor1-first=Robert Jr|editor2-last=Lopez|editor2-first=Donald S. Jr.|editor1-link=Robert Buswell Jr.|editor2-link=Donald S. Lopez, Jr.|title=Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism|page=737|date=2013|publisher=Princeton University Press|location=Princeton, NJ|isbn=9780691157863}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Gyohyo|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=955}}</ref> He took tonsure as a novice monk at the age of 14 and was given the ordination name "Saichō". Gyōhyō in turn was a disciple of {{ill|Dao-xuan|en|Dao-xuan|WD=Q11641588|lt=Dao-xuan}} (702–760, 道璿, Dōsen in Japanese), a prominent monk from China<ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Tao-Hsien|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=2215|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> of the Tiantai school who had brought the {{ill|East Mountain Teaching|en|East Mountain Teaching|WD=Q11526728|lt=East Mountain Teaching}} of {{ill|Chan Buddhism|en|Chan Buddhism|WD=Q940709|lt=Chan Buddhism}}, {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|WD=Q1198075|lt=Huayan}} teachings and the {{ill|Bodhisattva Precepts|en|Bodhisattva Precepts|WD=Q4936546|lt=Bodhisattva Precepts}} of the [[:en:Brahmajala Sutra (Mahayana)|''Brahmajala Sutra'']] to Japan in 736 and served as the "precept master" for ordination prior to the arrival of {{ill|Jianzhen|en|Jianzhen|WD=Q714061|lt=Jianzhen}}.<ref name="groner-book" />
By the age of 20, he undertook the full [[:en:Prātimokṣa|monastic precepts]] at the [[Tōdai-ji]], thus becoming a fully ordained monk in the official temple system. A few months later he abruptly retreated to {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}} for an intensive study and practice of Buddhism, though the exact reason for his departure remains unknown.<ref name="tendaishu" /><ref name="groner-book" /> Shortly after his retreat, he composed his {{nihongo|''Ganmon''|願文||"Saichō's Prayer"}} which included his personal vows to:<ref name="groner-book" /> # So long as I have not attained the stage where my six faculties are pure, I will not venture out into the world. # So long as I have not realized the absolute, I will not acquire any special skills or arts [e.g. medicine, divination, calligraphy, etc.]. # So long as I have not kept all the precepts purely, I will not participate in any lay donor's Buddhist meetings. # So long as I have not attained wisdom (lit. ''hannya'' 般若), I will not participate in worldly affairs unless it be to benefit others. # May any merit from my practice in the past, present and future be given not to me, but to all sentient beings so that they may attain supreme enlightenment.
In time, Saichō attracted other monks both on Mount Hiei, and from the Buddhist community in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara}}, and a monastic community developed on Mount Hiei, which eventually became [[Enryaku-ji]]. Saichō was said to have carved an image of the {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Bhaiṣajyaguru}} and enshrined it.<ref name="groner-book" /> Additionally, he lit a lamp of oil before the Buddha and prayed that the lamp would never be extinguished. This lamp is now known as the {{nihongo|''Fumetsu no Hōtō''|不滅の法灯||"Inextinguishable Dharma Lamp"}} and has remained lit for 1200 years.
The capital of Japan was moved from Nara to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] in 784, and then to {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} in 795. Because Mount Hiei was coincidentally located to the northeast of Kyoto, a direction considered dangerous according to {{ill|Feng shui|en|Feng shui|WD=Q170537|lt=Chinese geomancy}}, Saichō's presence on the mountain was thought to protect the new capital and brought him to the attention of the court. Saichō and his community on Mount Hiei also started to correspond and exchange ceremonies with the established communities in Nara, in addition to the monks at the Court, further enhancing his prestige.
One of Saichō's earliest supporters in the Court was Wake no Hiroyo, who invited Saichō to give lectures at Takaosan-ji along with fourteen other eminent monks. Saichō was not the first to be invited, indicating that he was still relatively unknown in the Court, but rising in prominence.<ref name="groner-book" />
=== Trip to China === [[File:Culto do chá p25.png|thumb|Saichō is known for having introduced tea to Japan]] The success of the Takaosanji lectures, plus Saichō's association with Wake no Hiroyo soon caught the attention of [[Emperor Kanmu]] who consulted with Saichō about propagating his Buddhist teachings further, and to help bridge the traditional rivalry between the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=East Asian Yogācāra}} and {{ill|East Asian Mādhyamaka|en|East Asian Mādhyamaka|WD=Q1206580|lt=East Asian Mādhyamaka}} schools.<ref name="groner-book" />
The emperor granted a petition by Saichō to journey to China to further study Tiantai doctrine in China and bring back more texts.<ref name="groner-book2">{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho : The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=38–64}}</ref> Saichō was expected to only remain in China for a short time however.
Saichō could read Chinese but was unable to speak it at all, thus he was allowed to bring a trusted disciple along named {{nihongo|Gishin|義眞}}, who apparently could speak Chinese. Gishin would later become one of the head monks of the Tendai order after Saichō.
Saichō was part of the four-ship {{ill|Japanese missions to Imperial China|en|Japanese missions to Imperial China|WD=Q15281711|lt=diplomatic mission to Tang China}} in 803. The ships were forced to turn back due to heavy winds, where they spent some time at {{ill|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|en|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|WD=Q728218|lt=Dazaifu, Fukuoka}}. During this time, Saichō likely met another passenger, {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}, a fellow Buddhist monk who was sent to China on a similar mission though he was expected to stay much longer.<ref name="groner-book2" />
When the ships set sail again, two sank during a heavy storm, but Saichō's ship arrived at the port of {{ill|Ningbo|en|Ningbo|WD=Q42780|lt=Ningbo}}, then known as Mingzhou ({{zh|c=明州| p=Míngzhōu}}), in northern {{ill|Zhejiang|en|Zhejiang|WD=Q16967|lt=Zhejiang}} in 804. Shortly after arrival, permission was granted for Saichō and his party to travel to {{ill|Tiantai Mountain|en|Tiantai Mountain|WD=Q1146118|lt=Tiantai Mountain}} and he was introduced to the seventh Patriarch of {{ill|Tiantai|en|Tiantai|WD=Q668188|lt=Tiantai}}, Daosui ({{zh|c=道邃|p=Dàosuì}}), who became his primary teacher during his time in China. Daosui was instrumental in teaching Saichō about Tiantai methods of meditation, monastic discipline and orthodox teachings.<ref name="groner-book2" /> Saichō remained under this instruction for approximately 135 days.
Saichō spent the next several months copying various Buddhist works with the intention of bringing them back to Japan with him. While some works existed in Japan already, Saichō felt that they suffered from copyist errors or other defects, and so he made fresh copies. Once the task was completed, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo, but the ship was harbored in {{ill|Fuzhou|en|Fuzhou|WD=Q68481|lt=Fuzhou}} at the time, and would not return for six weeks.
During this time, Saichō went to Yuezhou (越州, modern-day {{ill|Shaoxing|en|Shaoxing|WD=Q42666|lt=Shaoxing}}) and sought out texts and information on {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} (Esoteric) Buddhism. The Tiantai school originally only utilized "mixed" ({{nihongo|''zōmitsu''|雑密||}}) ceremonial practices, but over time esoteric Buddhism took on a greater role. By the time Saichō had arrived in China, a number of Tiantai Buddhist centers provided esoteric training, and both Saichō and Gishin received initiation at a temple in {{ill|Yue Prefecture (Zhejiang)|en|Yue Prefecture (Zhejiang)|WD=Q17164288|lt=Yue Prefecture}}. However, it's unclear what transmission or transmissions(s) they received. Some evidence suggests that Saichō did not receive the dual ({{nihongo|''ryōbu''|兩部||}} transmissions of the {{ill|Diamond Realm|en|Diamond Realm|WD=Q518314|lt=Diamond Realm}} and the {{ill|Womb Realm|en|Womb Realm|WD=Q855739|lt=Womb Realm}}.<ref name="groner-book2" /> Instead, it is thought he may have only received the Diamond Realm transmission, but the evidence is not conclusive one way or the other.
Finally, on the tenth day of the fifth month of 805, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo and after compiling further bibliographies, boarded the ship back for Japan and arrived in {{ill|Tsushima, Nagasaki|en|Tsushima, Nagasaki|WD=Q991032|lt=Tsushima}} on the fifth day of the sixth month. Although Saichō had only stayed in China for a total of eight months, his return was eagerly awaited by the court in Kyoto.
=== Founding of Tendai ===
On his return from China, Saichō worked hard to win recognition from the court and "in the first month of 806, Saichō's Tendai Lotus school (''Tendai-hokke-shū'' 天台法華宗) won official recognition when the court of the ailing emperor Kanmu issued another edict, this one permitting two annual ordinands (''nenbundosha'') for Saichō's new school on Mount Hiei. This edict states that, following Saichō's request, the ordinands would be divided between two curricula: the ''shanagō'' course, centering on the study of the Mahavairocana Sūtra (this was the Mikkyō curriculum, shana being the abbreviation for Birushana, the Japanese transliteration of Vairocana), and the shikangō course, based on the study of the ''Mo-ho chih-kuan'', the seminal work of the T'ien-t'ai patriarch Chih-i 智顗 (538–597) (this was the Tendai curriculum, ''shikan'' being the Japanese reading of Chih-i's central practice of ''chih-kuan'' [cessation and contemplation]) (''Kenkairon engi'', DZ 1, pp. 294–296). Thus from its very inception the Tendai Lotus school was equally based on Mikkyō and T'ien-t'ai. It was as a subdivision of Saichō's new school that Mikkyō first received the official acknowledgment of the imperial court and became a proper subject of study in Japanese Buddhism.
{{quote|[I]n 813 Saichō composed the ''Ehyō tendaishū'' (DZ 1, pp. 343–366), which argues that the principal Buddhist masters of China and Korea all relied on T'ien-t'ai doctrine in composing their own works. By identifying numerous references to and quotes from T'ien-t'ai treatises in the works of {{ill|Jizang|en|Jizang|WD=Q712287|lt=Chi-tsang}} 吉蔵 of the {{ill|East Asian Mādhyamaka|en|East Asian Mādhyamaka|WD=Q1206580|lt=San-lun}} 三論 school, Chih-chou of the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Fa-hsiang}} 法相 school, Fa-tsang of the {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|WD=Q1198075|lt=Huayen}} 華嚴 school, I-hsing of {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|WD=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō}}, and other prominent teachers, Saichō asserted that T'ien-t'ai formed the foundation for all major Buddhist schools in East Asia.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp">Abe Ryūichi: Saichō and Kūkai: A conflict of interpretations. Japanese Journal of Religious Studies Vol: 22/1–2, pp. 103–137, 1995. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090219104325/http://www.nanzan-u.ac.jp/SHUBUNKEN/publications/jjrs/pdf/438.pdf PDF]</ref>}}
Before Saichō, all monastic ordinations took place at [[Tōdai-ji]] temple under the ancient {{ill|Vinaya|en|Vinaya|WD=Q848764|lt=Vinaya}} code, but Saichō intended to found his school as a strictly {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}} institution and ordain monks using the Bodhisattva Precepts only. Despite intense opposition from the traditional Buddhist schools in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara}}, his request was granted by {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}} in 822, several days after his death. This was the fruit of years of effort and a formal debate.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>
=== Decline and Death === By 822, Saichō petitioned the court to allow the monks at Mount Hiei to ordain under the Bodhisattva Precepts rather than the traditional ordination system of the ''[[:en:Prātimokṣa|Prātimokṣa]]'', arguing that his community would be a purely {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}, not {{ill|Hinayana|en|Hinayana|WD=Q193814|lt=Hinayana}} one.<ref>{{cite book | last = Abe | first = Ryuichi | title = The Weaving of Mantra: Kukai and the Construction of Esoteric Buddhist Discourse | publisher = Columbia University Press | year = 1999 | isbn = 0-231-11286-6 | pages=40–44, 50–52}}</ref> This was met with strong protest by the Buddhist establishment who supported the ''kokubunji'' system, and lodged a protest. Saichō composed the {{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論||"A Clarification of the Precepts"}}, which stressed the significance of the Bodhisattva Precepts,<ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Saicho|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=319|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> but his request was still rejected until 7 days after his death at the age of 56.<ref name="tendaishu" />
== Relationship with Kūkai == Saichō traveled to China along with a number of other young monks, one of whom was named {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}. Saichō befriended him during his trip to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China}} who traveled with him going and coming. This turned out to be pivotal to the future development of Buddhism. {{quote|During the last month of his stay on Chinese soil, while awaiting the arrival of his ship at the port city of Ming-chou, Saichō traveled to Yüeh-chou to collect additional Buddhist texts. At Lung-hsing ssu 龍興寺 Saichō chanced to meet the priest Shun-hsiao"<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}, and likewise returned with esoteric ({{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric}}) Buddhist texts. Saichō was entranced with the new material and wanted to learn more. On the trip back he found that Kukai had studied these teachings in depth and had an entire library of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} materials. This friendship would influence the future of Tendai. {{quote|Saichō 最澄 and Kūkai 空海 are renowned as the founders, respectively, of the Japanese Tendai and Shingon schools, both of which grew into influential institutions of continuing importance even today. The two figures cooperated, moreover, in an effort to transplant the seed of esoteric Buddhism (mikkyō) to the cultural soil of Japan. Saichō, for example, prepared the way for Kūkai—still largely unrecognized after his return from T'ang China—to perform the Mikkyō initiation ritual of {{ill|Abhisheka|en|Abhisheka|WD=Q75799|lt=''abhiṣeka''}} (''kanjō'' 灌頂) for the high priests of the Nara Buddhist establishment and the dignitaries of the imperial" {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian court}}.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
It was Saichō who performed the ''abhiṣeka'', or initiatory ritual, for the court. {{quote|Saichō also endorsed the court's bequest to Kūkai of the mountain temple of {{ill|Jingo-ji|en|Jingo-ji|WD=Q1075034|lt=Takaosan-ji}} northwest of Kyoto as the first center for Kūkai's {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}. Kūkai, in turn, responded to Saichō's wish to incorporate Mikkyō into the eclectic system of Tendai by training Saichō and his disciples in the esoteric Buddhist rituals and by lending Saichō various Mikkyō texts that he had brought with him from China."<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
== The identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings == {{JapaneseBuddhism}} Thus esoteric Buddhism became an important aspect of the Tendai school, which was primarily focused on the {{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}}. However, unlike the {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon}} school (which saw esoteric practice as superior to the Lotus Sutra), Saichō held to the "identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings" (''enmitsu itchi'' 円密一致) which means there is a unity and agreement among the teachings of the Lotus Sutra and Esoteric Buddhism."<ref>Ōkubo Ryōshun 大久保良峻. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/4331 “The Identity between the Purport of the Perfect and Esoteric Teachings.”] ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 41/1 (2014): 83–102.</ref> Saichō, in a letter to Kukai, wrote:<ref name=":4">Ryuichi Abe. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/2562 ''Saichō and Kūkai: A Conflict of Interpretations Ryuichi Abe.''] Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 1995 22/1-2</ref><blockquote>But the {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana}} school (''shanashu'' 遮那宗) and Tendai interfuse with one another. They also share the same commentary.... There should be no such thing as preferring one to the other. The Lotus and the {{ill|Golden Light Sutra|en|Golden Light Sutra|WD=Q391694|lt=Golden Light}} are those texts to which the previous emperor [<nowiki/>[[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]]] devoted himself, and there exists no difference between the One Unifying Vehicle [of Tendai] and Shingon.</blockquote>Paul Groner states, {{quote|Chinese T'ien-t'ai had been a syncretistic tradition, particularly at the T'ien-t'ai Yu-ch'uan monastery. Chinese monks had been interested in Ch'an and Esoteric Buddhism as well as in the Ssu-fen la and Fan wang precepts. Saichō inherited this tradition, but developed certain aspects of it in innovative ways. For example, Saichō considered Esoteric Buddhism to be essentially the same as Tendai (enmitsu itchi) and thus awarded Esoteric Buddhism a more central place in the Tendai tradition than it had been given by most Chinese monks. Like Kūkai, Saichō emphasized the importance of striving for enlightenment as an immediate goal to be attained in this existence (''sokushin-jōbutsu'').<ref>Groner, Paul (1989). "The Lotus Sutra and Saicho's Interpretation of the Realization of Buddhahood with This Very Body". In Tanabe, George J.; Tanabe, Willa Jane (ed.). The Lotus Sutra in Japanese Culture. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. {{ISBN|0-8248-1198-4}}. pp. 61–62</ref>}} Tendai and Esoteric practices, he felt, provided a direct path (''jikidō'') to enlightenment, whereas the teachings of the Nara schools required aeons to bring the practitioner to enlightenment.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite news | last = Groner | first = Paul | title = Short History of Dengyo Daishi | url = http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060503031218/http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-date = 2006-05-03}}</ref>
However, {{quote|During the years that Saichō studied Esoteric Buddhism (from 805–815), more than half of the Tendai yearly ordinands left Mount Hiei. Many of them defected to the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Hosso school}}; others departed in order to study Esoteric Buddhism with Kūkai or to support their ailing mothers. It became clear that if Tendai were to survive, Saichō would have to retain many more of his students on Mount Hiei.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>}} Moreover, Saichō began to realize that his own idea of "enmitsu itchi" was not exactly shared by the esoteric Shingon school, and especially its founder Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi).
Ryuichi Abe writes, {{quote|[W]hat makes the relationship between Saichō and Kūkai decisive in Japanese Buddhist history is not so much their cooperation as the manner in which it came to an end. Their alliance began to deteriorate when Saichō, after receiving abhiseka from Kūkai, hurried back to Mount Hiei, where the work of laying the foundation of the new Tendai school awaited him. Saichō continued to study and copy Mikkyō texts borrowed from Kūkai, but despite Kūkai's repeated requests he did not return to Takaosan-ji to resume his studies. Their rapport finally terminated when Kūkai harshly condemned Saichō's approach to Mikkyō as a transgression of the esoteric precept of samaya [the promise to keep the oral/esoteric teachings private], and Saichō retorted by denouncing Kūkai's manner of instruction<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}} {{quote|Thus it was Mikkyō that brought Saichō and Kūkai together; it was also Mikkyō that drove them apart. The break between Saichō and Kūkai left a long-lasting legacy in the Tendai and Shingon schools, whose complex relationship, constantly oscillating between affiliation and rivalry, shaped the contours of Buddhist history in the Heian period.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}} {{quote|During the last five or six years of his life, Saicho strove to secure the place of Tendai within Japanese Buddhism, and in the process composed almost all of his major works.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>}} {{quote|In 816, Saichō added a new introduction to the work. This introduction chides Sanron, Hossō, and Kegon—the leading schools of Nara Buddhism—for ignoring the influence of T'ien-t'ai on the works of their Chinese patriarchs, but its criticism of Shingon stands out: "The esoteric Shingon Buddhist, the newcomer, went so far as to deny the validity of transmission through writing (hitsuju Ù4)" (DZ 3, p. 344). In this comment Saichō denounced Kūkai and Shingon for their approach to Buddhism and religious study."<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
Saichō's late life criticisms were ignored by his own leading disciples, and the Tendai would continue to teach Mikkyō and [[Buddhist meditation#Tiantai .C5.9Bamatha-vipa.C5.9Byan.C4.81|Shikangō]] (''śamatha-vipaśyanā''). Saichō's public condemnation of Kūkai would later form the seeds for some of the criticisms leveled by {{ill|Nichiren|en|Nichiren|WD=Q311478|lt=Nichiren}} (1222–1282), the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|en|Nichiren Buddhism|WD=Q871371|lt=Nichiren Buddhism}}, who would cite that work in his own debates in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}.<ref>Gosho | http://www.sgilibrary.org/view.php?page=565</ref>{{better source needed|date=July 2024}}
Saichō was also an author. He wrote a number of texts, the main ones include: *{{nihongo|''Shōgon Jikkyō''|照権実鏡|}} (817) *{{nihongo|''Sange Gakushō Shiki''|山家学生式|}} (818–819) *{{nihongo|''Shugo Kokkai Shō''|守護国界章|}} (818) *{{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論|}} (820)

{{ill|calligrapher|WD=Q3303330}}; {{ill|philosopher|WD=Q4964182}}|father={{ill|Mitsuno Momoe|WD=Q118750033}}|notable_works={{ill|An Essay on the Protection of the Nation|WD=Q11450104}}; {{ill|The Regulations for the Students of the Mountain School|WD=Q134271462}}|religion={{ill|Tendai|WD=Q855964}}|native_name=最澄|resting_place={{ill|Enryaku-ji|WD=Q917195}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q449943]] Wikidata name: Saichō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:00, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|8/9th-century Japanese Buddhist monk; founder of the Tendai sect}} {{Over-quotation|date=July 2024}} {{Infobox religious biography |name = Saichō (最澄) |image= 最澄像 一乗寺蔵 平安時代.jpg |caption = Painting of Saichō |birth_date = September 15, 767 |birth_place = |death_date = June 26, 822 (age 54) | religion = {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} |school = {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} |title = Founder of {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai Buddhism}} |teacher = Gyōhyō (行表) |successor = Gishin (義真) }} {{nihongo|'''Saichō'''|最澄||September 15, 767 – June 26, 822}} was a {{ill|Japanese people|en|Japanese people|WD=Q161652|lt=Japanese}} {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=Buddhist monk}} credited with founding the {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} school of Buddhism based on the Chinese {{ill|Tiantai|en|Tiantai|WD=Q668188|lt=Tiantai}} school he was exposed to during his trip to {{ill|Tang dynasty|en|Tang dynasty|WD=Q9683|lt=Tang China}} beginning in 804. He founded the temple and headquarters of Tendai at [[Enryaku-ji]] on {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}} near {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}. He is also said to have been the first to bring {{ill|History of tea in Japan|en|History of tea in Japan|WD=Q6579892|lt=tea}} to Japan. After his death, he was awarded the posthumous title of '''Dengyō Daishi''' (伝教大師).
== Life ==
=== Early life ===
Saichō was born in the year 767 in the city of Ōmi, in present {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|WD=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}, with the given name of Hirono.<ref name="tendaishu">{{cite web|title=Tendai Homepage: Dengyo Daishi's Life and Teachings|url=http://www.tendai.or.jp/english/index.php|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> According to family tradition, Saichō's ancestors were descendants of {{ill|Emperor of China|en|Emperor of China|WD=Q268218|lt=emperors}} of [[Han dynasty#Eastern Han|Eastern Han China]];<ref name="tendaishu" /> however, no positive evidence exists for this claim. The region where Saichō was born did have a large Chinese immigrant population, so Saichō likely did have Chinese ancestry.<ref name="groner-book">{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho: The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=17–37}}</ref>
During Saichō's time, the Buddhist temples in Japan were officially organized into a national network known as the {{ill|Provincial temple|en|Provincial temple|WD=Q1207757|lt=Provincial temple}} system, and at the age of 13, Saichō became a disciple of one Gyōhyō (722–797, 行表).<ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Buswell|editor1-first=Robert Jr|editor2-last=Lopez|editor2-first=Donald S. Jr.|editor1-link=Robert Buswell Jr.|editor2-link=Donald S. Lopez, Jr.|title=Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism|page=737|date=2013|publisher=Princeton University Press|location=Princeton, NJ|isbn=9780691157863}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Gyohyo|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=955}}</ref> He took tonsure as a novice monk at the age of 14 and was given the ordination name "Saichō". Gyōhyō in turn was a disciple of {{ill|Dao-xuan|en|Dao-xuan|WD=Q11641588|lt=Dao-xuan}} (702–760, 道璿, Dōsen in Japanese), a prominent monk from China<ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Tao-Hsien|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=2215|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> of the Tiantai school who had brought the {{ill|East Mountain Teaching|en|East Mountain Teaching|WD=Q11526728|lt=East Mountain Teaching}} of {{ill|Chan Buddhism|en|Chan Buddhism|WD=Q940709|lt=Chan Buddhism}}, {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|WD=Q1198075|lt=Huayan}} teachings and the {{ill|Bodhisattva Precepts|en|Bodhisattva Precepts|WD=Q4936546|lt=Bodhisattva Precepts}} of the [[:en:Brahmajala Sutra (Mahayana)|''Brahmajala Sutra'']] to Japan in 736 and served as the "precept master" for ordination prior to the arrival of {{ill|Jianzhen|en|Jianzhen|WD=Q714061|lt=Jianzhen}}.<ref name="groner-book" />
By the age of 20, he undertook the full [[:en:Prātimokṣa|monastic precepts]] at the [[Tōdai-ji]], thus becoming a fully ordained monk in the official temple system. A few months later he abruptly retreated to {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|WD=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}} for an intensive study and practice of Buddhism, though the exact reason for his departure remains unknown.<ref name="tendaishu" /><ref name="groner-book" /> Shortly after his retreat, he composed his {{nihongo|''Ganmon''|願文||"Saichō's Prayer"}} which included his personal vows to:<ref name="groner-book" /> # So long as I have not attained the stage where my six faculties are pure, I will not venture out into the world. # So long as I have not realized the absolute, I will not acquire any special skills or arts [e.g. medicine, divination, calligraphy, etc.]. # So long as I have not kept all the precepts purely, I will not participate in any lay donor's Buddhist meetings. # So long as I have not attained wisdom (lit. ''hannya'' 般若), I will not participate in worldly affairs unless it be to benefit others. # May any merit from my practice in the past, present and future be given not to me, but to all sentient beings so that they may attain supreme enlightenment.
In time, Saichō attracted other monks both on Mount Hiei, and from the Buddhist community in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara}}, and a monastic community developed on Mount Hiei, which eventually became [[Enryaku-ji]]. Saichō was said to have carved an image of the {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|WD=Q854773|lt=Bhaiṣajyaguru}} and enshrined it.<ref name="groner-book" /> Additionally, he lit a lamp of oil before the Buddha and prayed that the lamp would never be extinguished. This lamp is now known as the {{nihongo|''Fumetsu no Hōtō''|不滅の法灯||"Inextinguishable Dharma Lamp"}} and has remained lit for 1200 years.
The capital of Japan was moved from Nara to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] in 784, and then to {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}} in 795. Because Mount Hiei was coincidentally located to the northeast of Kyoto, a direction considered dangerous according to {{ill|Feng shui|en|Feng shui|WD=Q170537|lt=Chinese geomancy}}, Saichō's presence on the mountain was thought to protect the new capital and brought him to the attention of the court. Saichō and his community on Mount Hiei also started to correspond and exchange ceremonies with the established communities in Nara, in addition to the monks at the Court, further enhancing his prestige.
One of Saichō's earliest supporters in the Court was Wake no Hiroyo, who invited Saichō to give lectures at Takaosan-ji along with fourteen other eminent monks. Saichō was not the first to be invited, indicating that he was still relatively unknown in the Court, but rising in prominence.<ref name="groner-book" />
=== Trip to China === [[File:Culto do chá p25.png|thumb|Saichō is known for having introduced tea to Japan]] The success of the Takaosanji lectures, plus Saichō's association with Wake no Hiroyo soon caught the attention of [[Emperor Kanmu]] who consulted with Saichō about propagating his Buddhist teachings further, and to help bridge the traditional rivalry between the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=East Asian Yogācāra}} and {{ill|East Asian Mādhyamaka|en|East Asian Mādhyamaka|WD=Q1206580|lt=East Asian Mādhyamaka}} schools.<ref name="groner-book" />
The emperor granted a petition by Saichō to journey to China to further study Tiantai doctrine in China and bring back more texts.<ref name="groner-book2">{{cite book|last=Groner|first=Paul|title=Saicho : The Establishment of the Japanese Tendai School|year=2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=0824823710|pages=38–64}}</ref> Saichō was expected to only remain in China for a short time however.
Saichō could read Chinese but was unable to speak it at all, thus he was allowed to bring a trusted disciple along named {{nihongo|Gishin|義眞}}, who apparently could speak Chinese. Gishin would later become one of the head monks of the Tendai order after Saichō.
Saichō was part of the four-ship {{ill|Japanese missions to Imperial China|en|Japanese missions to Imperial China|WD=Q15281711|lt=diplomatic mission to Tang China}} in 803. The ships were forced to turn back due to heavy winds, where they spent some time at {{ill|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|en|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|WD=Q728218|lt=Dazaifu, Fukuoka}}. During this time, Saichō likely met another passenger, {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}, a fellow Buddhist monk who was sent to China on a similar mission though he was expected to stay much longer.<ref name="groner-book2" />
When the ships set sail again, two sank during a heavy storm, but Saichō's ship arrived at the port of {{ill|Ningbo|en|Ningbo|WD=Q42780|lt=Ningbo}}, then known as Mingzhou ({{zh|c=明州| p=Míngzhōu}}), in northern {{ill|Zhejiang|en|Zhejiang|WD=Q16967|lt=Zhejiang}} in 804. Shortly after arrival, permission was granted for Saichō and his party to travel to {{ill|Tiantai Mountain|en|Tiantai Mountain|WD=Q1146118|lt=Tiantai Mountain}} and he was introduced to the seventh Patriarch of {{ill|Tiantai|en|Tiantai|WD=Q668188|lt=Tiantai}}, Daosui ({{zh|c=道邃|p=Dàosuì}}), who became his primary teacher during his time in China. Daosui was instrumental in teaching Saichō about Tiantai methods of meditation, monastic discipline and orthodox teachings.<ref name="groner-book2" /> Saichō remained under this instruction for approximately 135 days.
Saichō spent the next several months copying various Buddhist works with the intention of bringing them back to Japan with him. While some works existed in Japan already, Saichō felt that they suffered from copyist errors or other defects, and so he made fresh copies. Once the task was completed, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo, but the ship was harbored in {{ill|Fuzhou|en|Fuzhou|WD=Q68481|lt=Fuzhou}} at the time, and would not return for six weeks.
During this time, Saichō went to Yuezhou (越州, modern-day {{ill|Shaoxing|en|Shaoxing|WD=Q42666|lt=Shaoxing}}) and sought out texts and information on {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} (Esoteric) Buddhism. The Tiantai school originally only utilized "mixed" ({{nihongo|''zōmitsu''|雑密||}}) ceremonial practices, but over time esoteric Buddhism took on a greater role. By the time Saichō had arrived in China, a number of Tiantai Buddhist centers provided esoteric training, and both Saichō and Gishin received initiation at a temple in {{ill|Yue Prefecture (Zhejiang)|en|Yue Prefecture (Zhejiang)|WD=Q17164288|lt=Yue Prefecture}}. However, it's unclear what transmission or transmissions(s) they received. Some evidence suggests that Saichō did not receive the dual ({{nihongo|''ryōbu''|兩部||}} transmissions of the {{ill|Diamond Realm|en|Diamond Realm|WD=Q518314|lt=Diamond Realm}} and the {{ill|Womb Realm|en|Womb Realm|WD=Q855739|lt=Womb Realm}}.<ref name="groner-book2" /> Instead, it is thought he may have only received the Diamond Realm transmission, but the evidence is not conclusive one way or the other.
Finally, on the tenth day of the fifth month of 805, Saichō and his party returned to Ningbo and after compiling further bibliographies, boarded the ship back for Japan and arrived in {{ill|Tsushima, Nagasaki|en|Tsushima, Nagasaki|WD=Q991032|lt=Tsushima}} on the fifth day of the sixth month. Although Saichō had only stayed in China for a total of eight months, his return was eagerly awaited by the court in Kyoto.
=== Founding of Tendai ===
On his return from China, Saichō worked hard to win recognition from the court and "in the first month of 806, Saichō's Tendai Lotus school (''Tendai-hokke-shū'' 天台法華宗) won official recognition when the court of the ailing emperor Kanmu issued another edict, this one permitting two annual ordinands (''nenbundosha'') for Saichō's new school on Mount Hiei. This edict states that, following Saichō's request, the ordinands would be divided between two curricula: the ''shanagō'' course, centering on the study of the Mahavairocana Sūtra (this was the Mikkyō curriculum, shana being the abbreviation for Birushana, the Japanese transliteration of Vairocana), and the shikangō course, based on the study of the ''Mo-ho chih-kuan'', the seminal work of the T'ien-t'ai patriarch Chih-i 智顗 (538–597) (this was the Tendai curriculum, ''shikan'' being the Japanese reading of Chih-i's central practice of ''chih-kuan'' [cessation and contemplation]) (''Kenkairon engi'', DZ 1, pp. 294–296). Thus from its very inception the Tendai Lotus school was equally based on Mikkyō and T'ien-t'ai. It was as a subdivision of Saichō's new school that Mikkyō first received the official acknowledgment of the imperial court and became a proper subject of study in Japanese Buddhism.
{{quote|[I]n 813 Saichō composed the ''Ehyō tendaishū'' (DZ 1, pp. 343–366), which argues that the principal Buddhist masters of China and Korea all relied on T'ien-t'ai doctrine in composing their own works. By identifying numerous references to and quotes from T'ien-t'ai treatises in the works of {{ill|Jizang|en|Jizang|WD=Q712287|lt=Chi-tsang}} 吉蔵 of the {{ill|East Asian Mādhyamaka|en|East Asian Mādhyamaka|WD=Q1206580|lt=San-lun}} 三論 school, Chih-chou of the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Fa-hsiang}} 法相 school, Fa-tsang of the {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|WD=Q1198075|lt=Huayen}} 華嚴 school, I-hsing of {{ill|Mikkyō|en|Mikkyō|WD=Q336102|lt=Mikkyō}}, and other prominent teachers, Saichō asserted that T'ien-t'ai formed the foundation for all major Buddhist schools in East Asia.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp">Abe Ryūichi: Saichō and Kūkai: A conflict of interpretations. Japanese Journal of Religious Studies Vol: 22/1–2, pp. 103–137, 1995. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090219104325/http://www.nanzan-u.ac.jp/SHUBUNKEN/publications/jjrs/pdf/438.pdf PDF]</ref>}}
Before Saichō, all monastic ordinations took place at [[Tōdai-ji]] temple under the ancient {{ill|Vinaya|en|Vinaya|WD=Q848764|lt=Vinaya}} code, but Saichō intended to found his school as a strictly {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}} institution and ordain monks using the Bodhisattva Precepts only. Despite intense opposition from the traditional Buddhist schools in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara}}, his request was granted by {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|WD=Q316654|lt=Emperor Saga}} in 822, several days after his death. This was the fruit of years of effort and a formal debate.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>
=== Decline and Death === By 822, Saichō petitioned the court to allow the monks at Mount Hiei to ordain under the Bodhisattva Precepts rather than the traditional ordination system of the ''[[:en:Prātimokṣa|Prātimokṣa]]'', arguing that his community would be a purely {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}, not {{ill|Hinayana|en|Hinayana|WD=Q193814|lt=Hinayana}} one.<ref>{{cite book | last = Abe | first = Ryuichi | title = The Weaving of Mantra: Kukai and the Construction of Esoteric Buddhist Discourse | publisher = Columbia University Press | year = 1999 | isbn = 0-231-11286-6 | pages=40–44, 50–52}}</ref> This was met with strong protest by the Buddhist establishment who supported the ''kokubunji'' system, and lodged a protest. Saichō composed the {{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論||"A Clarification of the Precepts"}}, which stressed the significance of the Bodhisattva Precepts,<ref>{{cite web|title=The Soka Gakkai Dictionary of Buddhism: Saicho|url=http://www.sgilibrary.org/search_dict.php?id=319|access-date=10 December 2012}}</ref> but his request was still rejected until 7 days after his death at the age of 56.<ref name="tendaishu" />
== Relationship with Kūkai == Saichō traveled to China along with a number of other young monks, one of whom was named {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|WD=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}}. Saichō befriended him during his trip to {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China}} who traveled with him going and coming. This turned out to be pivotal to the future development of Buddhism. {{quote|During the last month of his stay on Chinese soil, while awaiting the arrival of his ship at the port city of Ming-chou, Saichō traveled to Yüeh-chou to collect additional Buddhist texts. At Lung-hsing ssu 龍興寺 Saichō chanced to meet the priest Shun-hsiao"<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}, and likewise returned with esoteric ({{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=tantric}}) Buddhist texts. Saichō was entranced with the new material and wanted to learn more. On the trip back he found that Kukai had studied these teachings in depth and had an entire library of {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} materials. This friendship would influence the future of Tendai. {{quote|Saichō 最澄 and Kūkai 空海 are renowned as the founders, respectively, of the Japanese Tendai and Shingon schools, both of which grew into influential institutions of continuing importance even today. The two figures cooperated, moreover, in an effort to transplant the seed of esoteric Buddhism (mikkyō) to the cultural soil of Japan. Saichō, for example, prepared the way for Kūkai—still largely unrecognized after his return from T'ang China—to perform the Mikkyō initiation ritual of {{ill|Abhisheka|en|Abhisheka|WD=Q75799|lt=''abhiṣeka''}} (''kanjō'' 灌頂) for the high priests of the Nara Buddhist establishment and the dignitaries of the imperial" {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian court}}.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
It was Saichō who performed the ''abhiṣeka'', or initiatory ritual, for the court. {{quote|Saichō also endorsed the court's bequest to Kūkai of the mountain temple of {{ill|Jingo-ji|en|Jingo-ji|WD=Q1075034|lt=Takaosan-ji}} northwest of Kyoto as the first center for Kūkai's {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}. Kūkai, in turn, responded to Saichō's wish to incorporate Mikkyō into the eclectic system of Tendai by training Saichō and his disciples in the esoteric Buddhist rituals and by lending Saichō various Mikkyō texts that he had brought with him from China."<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
== The identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings == {{JapaneseBuddhism}} Thus esoteric Buddhism became an important aspect of the Tendai school, which was primarily focused on the {{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}}. However, unlike the {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon}} school (which saw esoteric practice as superior to the Lotus Sutra), Saichō held to the "identity of the purport of Perfect and Esoteric teachings" (''enmitsu itchi'' 円密一致) which means there is a unity and agreement among the teachings of the Lotus Sutra and Esoteric Buddhism."<ref>Ōkubo Ryōshun 大久保良峻. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/4331 “The Identity between the Purport of the Perfect and Esoteric Teachings.”] ''Japanese Journal of Religious Studies'' 41/1 (2014): 83–102.</ref> Saichō, in a letter to Kukai, wrote:<ref name=":4">Ryuichi Abe. [https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/nfile/2562 ''Saichō and Kūkai: A Conflict of Interpretations Ryuichi Abe.''] Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 1995 22/1-2</ref><blockquote>But the {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana}} school (''shanashu'' 遮那宗) and Tendai interfuse with one another. They also share the same commentary.... There should be no such thing as preferring one to the other. The Lotus and the {{ill|Golden Light Sutra|en|Golden Light Sutra|WD=Q391694|lt=Golden Light}} are those texts to which the previous emperor [<nowiki/>[[Emperor Kanmu|Kanmu]]] devoted himself, and there exists no difference between the One Unifying Vehicle [of Tendai] and Shingon.</blockquote>Paul Groner states, {{quote|Chinese T'ien-t'ai had been a syncretistic tradition, particularly at the T'ien-t'ai Yu-ch'uan monastery. Chinese monks had been interested in Ch'an and Esoteric Buddhism as well as in the Ssu-fen la and Fan wang precepts. Saichō inherited this tradition, but developed certain aspects of it in innovative ways. For example, Saichō considered Esoteric Buddhism to be essentially the same as Tendai (enmitsu itchi) and thus awarded Esoteric Buddhism a more central place in the Tendai tradition than it had been given by most Chinese monks. Like Kūkai, Saichō emphasized the importance of striving for enlightenment as an immediate goal to be attained in this existence (''sokushin-jōbutsu'').<ref>Groner, Paul (1989). "The Lotus Sutra and Saicho's Interpretation of the Realization of Buddhahood with This Very Body". In Tanabe, George J.; Tanabe, Willa Jane (ed.). The Lotus Sutra in Japanese Culture. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. {{ISBN|0-8248-1198-4}}. pp. 61–62</ref>}} Tendai and Esoteric practices, he felt, provided a direct path (''jikidō'') to enlightenment, whereas the teachings of the Nara schools required aeons to bring the practitioner to enlightenment.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite news | last = Groner | first = Paul | title = Short History of Dengyo Daishi | url = http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060503031218/http://www.tendai-us.org/ShortHistoryofDengyoDaishi.pdf| archive-date = 2006-05-03}}</ref>
However, {{quote|During the years that Saichō studied Esoteric Buddhism (from 805–815), more than half of the Tendai yearly ordinands left Mount Hiei. Many of them defected to the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Hosso school}}; others departed in order to study Esoteric Buddhism with Kūkai or to support their ailing mothers. It became clear that if Tendai were to survive, Saichō would have to retain many more of his students on Mount Hiei.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>}} Moreover, Saichō began to realize that his own idea of "enmitsu itchi" was not exactly shared by the esoteric Shingon school, and especially its founder Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi).
Ryuichi Abe writes, {{quote|[W]hat makes the relationship between Saichō and Kūkai decisive in Japanese Buddhist history is not so much their cooperation as the manner in which it came to an end. Their alliance began to deteriorate when Saichō, after receiving abhiseka from Kūkai, hurried back to Mount Hiei, where the work of laying the foundation of the new Tendai school awaited him. Saichō continued to study and copy Mikkyō texts borrowed from Kūkai, but despite Kūkai's repeated requests he did not return to Takaosan-ji to resume his studies. Their rapport finally terminated when Kūkai harshly condemned Saichō's approach to Mikkyō as a transgression of the esoteric precept of samaya [the promise to keep the oral/esoteric teachings private], and Saichō retorted by denouncing Kūkai's manner of instruction<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}} {{quote|Thus it was Mikkyō that brought Saichō and Kūkai together; it was also Mikkyō that drove them apart. The break between Saichō and Kūkai left a long-lasting legacy in the Tendai and Shingon schools, whose complex relationship, constantly oscillating between affiliation and rivalry, shaped the contours of Buddhist history in the Heian period.<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}} {{quote|During the last five or six years of his life, Saicho strove to secure the place of Tendai within Japanese Buddhism, and in the process composed almost all of his major works.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>}} {{quote|In 816, Saichō added a new introduction to the work. This introduction chides Sanron, Hossō, and Kegon—the leading schools of Nara Buddhism—for ignoring the influence of T'ien-t'ai on the works of their Chinese patriarchs, but its criticism of Shingon stands out: "The esoteric Shingon Buddhist, the newcomer, went so far as to deny the validity of transmission through writing (hitsuju Ù4)" (DZ 3, p. 344). In this comment Saichō denounced Kūkai and Shingon for their approach to Buddhism and religious study."<ref name="nanzan-u.ac.jp"/>}}
Saichō's late life criticisms were ignored by his own leading disciples, and the Tendai would continue to teach Mikkyō and [[Buddhist meditation#Tiantai .C5.9Bamatha-vipa.C5.9Byan.C4.81|Shikangō]] (''śamatha-vipaśyanā''). Saichō's public condemnation of Kūkai would later form the seeds for some of the criticisms leveled by {{ill|Nichiren|en|Nichiren|WD=Q311478|lt=Nichiren}} (1222–1282), the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|en|Nichiren Buddhism|WD=Q871371|lt=Nichiren Buddhism}}, who would cite that work in his own debates in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}.<ref>Gosho | http://www.sgilibrary.org/view.php?page=565</ref>{{better source needed|date=July 2024}}
Saichō was also an author. He wrote a number of texts, the main ones include: *{{nihongo|''Shōgon Jikkyō''|照権実鏡|}} (817) *{{nihongo|''Sange Gakushō Shiki''|山家学生式|}} (818–819) *{{nihongo|''Shugo Kokkai Shō''|守護国界章|}} (818) *{{nihongo|''Kenkairon''|顕戒論|}} (820)
